medical.title: New gene discovery could help identify better stem cell donors
medical.summary: Research from stem cell charity Anthony Nolan, published in Transplantation and Cellular Therapy, has revealed that 1 in 50 people studied has an "especially useful" gene variant that could make them a particularly desirable stem cell donor.

medical.title: Why repeated exposures may make allergies worse
medical.summary: A new preclinical study led by investigators from Mass General Brigham offers a potential explanation for two longstanding questions in allergy: Why do allergies often emerge only after repeated exposure, and why do people with one allergy frequently develop others? The findings are published in Immunity.

medical.title: AI assistant learns from radiology reports to spot problems in abdominal scans
medical.summary: An abdominal CT scan packs an extraordinary amount of information into a single image, layering dozens of organs and hundreds of possible conditions. It's widely considered one of the most complex scans in medicine to read, and even expert radiologists need time to carefully untangle what they're looking at. To help ease some of their workload, researchers presented a new AI assistant called RADAR (Rapid Abdominal Diagnosis with AI and Radiology).

medical.title: Medicine leaflets are failing patients—and sometimes frightening them
medical.summary: Patient information leaflets are meant to help people use their medicines safely. But many people find them confusing, overwhelming or even frightening. If a document designed to keep people safe ends up putting them off their treatment, it's a sign that something isn't working.

medical.title: Changing the way we age: Discovery could help preserve muscle strength
medical.summary: A groundbreaking discovery at the University of Missouri could help older adults maintain the muscle strength they need to stay active and independent, whether that means safely crossing the street or playing with their grandchildren.

medical.title: Lower spinal bone density may flag people at risk for cognitive decline
medical.summary: Researchers at Johns Hopkins University found that lower bone mineral density in the spine was associated with faster cognitive decline and accelerated age-related white matter injury, according to a study published in Radiology.

medical.title: Coffee doesn’t have to keep you awake to disrupt your sleep
medical.summary: Caffeine may make sleep less restorative even when you fall asleep normally and stay in bed for eight hours, with EEG recordings revealing fewer of the slow brain waves associated with deep sleep. Individual sensitivity varies dramatically, meaning even caffeine consumed earlier in the day could affect nighttime recovery for some people.

medical.title: 'Reporter game' helps regulate sensory-brain activity in autistic youth, MRI study finds
medical.summary: For many autistic children, everyday sensations such as the feel of scratchy fabric or a loud car alarm can be intensely distressing. Known as sensory over-responsivity, this common symptom can affect all aspects of everyday life, from school and family life to friendships, yet few research-based treatments exist.

medical.title: Varenicline and combination nicotine replacement therapy deemed preferred treatments for tobacco use
medical.summary: A new clinical practice guideline from the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) and Department of Defense (DoD) provides recommendations for tobacco use treatment. Tobacco and nicotine use among veterans and military service members causes physical and mental health effects and reduces force readiness.

medical.title: Women with enlarged breast tissue more likely to experience chronic migraine, neck pain and sleep apnea
medical.summary: Women with enlarged breast tissue, known medically as macromastia, may be more likely to experience chronic migraine, neck pain, certain spinal nerve disorders and obstructive sleep apnea, according to a new study by Wake Forest University School of Medicine researchers, published Tuesday in the journal Headache.

medical.title: Engineered probiotic bacteria produce cancer drugs inside tumors
medical.summary: E. coli in uncooked meat can cause diarrhea and food poisoning. Scientists, however, have found a way to turn the bacterium into a delivery agent that takes drugs straight to a tumor and transforms it into a tiny cancer drug dispensary.

medical.title: More than a third of positive tests for mpox may have been false diagnoses
medical.summary: In August 2024, the World Health Organization declared the mpox upsurge in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and its spread to neighboring countries a Public Health Emergency of International Concern. The emergence of a new strain and its rapid spread across eastern DRC, and later to other African countries and beyond, made reliable diagnosis essential for understanding the scale of the epidemic and guiding vaccination and other public health measures.

medical.title: What kind of a person am I? How fear and rejection can underpin OCD
medical.summary: When you think about obsessive-compulsive disorder, or OCD, does being a "neat freak" or "germophobe" come to mind?

medical.title: Study identifies estrogen receptor as key protector of the right heart in pulmonary hypertension
medical.summary: Researchers at National Jewish Health have identified a key way estrogen receptor alpha (ERα) helps protect the right side of the heart in pulmonary hypertension. The preclinical findings reveal that ERα preserves the survival and movement of endothelial cells, which line blood vessels, allowing the stressed heart to maintain the small vessels it needs to function.

medical.title: Researchers highlight how brain economy principles could transform clinical care
medical.summary: Researchers from The University of Texas Medical Branch (UTMB) are helping advance a growing global movement that reimagines health care through the lens of brain health.

medical.title: Patients with chronic pain may benefit from group medical visits
medical.summary: More than one in five U.S. adults lives with chronic pain, which isolation and stigma can worsen. Group medical visits allow multiple patients with a common condition to receive care alongside health education and peer support.

medical.title: Scientists find a natural gut compound that helps heal the intestine
medical.summary: A natural compound produced by gut bacteria after digesting foods such as pomegranates, walnuts, and berries may help repair and protect the intestinal lining. The discovery reveals a surprising beneficial side of an inflammatory pathway and could inspire more targeted treatments for Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis.

medical.title: Textbooks may have misdrawn this basic brain structure for 100 years
medical.summary: Scientists discovered that brain-cell axons may not be smooth tubes as textbooks have shown for more than a century, but instead naturally resemble strings of tiny pearls. Those pearl-like structures can change with neural activity and may help control how quickly electrical signals travel through the brain.

medical.title: 51 ways to get the planet tipping the right way
medical.summary: Researchers have identified 51 environmental solutions to save the planet. Here are five of the most promising The post 51 ways to get the planet tipping the right way appeared first on Positive News .

medical.title: What went right this week: solutions to save the world, plus more
medical.summary: Solutions to save the planet, protecting childhood from algorithms, and the new world map, plus more The post What went right this week: solutions to save the world, plus more appeared first on Positive News .

science.title: Hurricane Polo strengthens to top Category 5 off Mexico
science.summary: Hurricane Polo reached maximum Category 5 strength off Mexico's Pacific coast Tuesday but is expected to stay at sea, the U.S. National Hurricane Center (NHC) said.

science.title: Respiratory problems climb past 170,000 cases in haze-hit Indonesia
science.summary: More than 170,000 respiratory cases were recorded in regions affected by haze in Indonesia, a Health Ministry official said Tuesday, as the country has battled for weeks to control fires that caused the toxic smog.

science.title: New tool aims to deliver graziers a faster, more accurate read on exactly how much feed is in front of their cattle
science.summary: A drone lifts off over a paddock at Boorowa Agricultural Research Station, the breeze from its rotors setting the tall, uncut grass below rippling. At the controls, Stuart Brown, a senior research technician at CSIRO, keeps a careful eye on the attached LiDAR (Light Detection and Ranging) sensor as it fires an invisible lattice of laser pulses at the grass, building a three-dimensional map of the paddock, one small cube of space at a time.

science.title: A tiny chariot fitting reveals Egyptian glass reached Iron Age Britain
science.summary: At the end of last year, curators from the Ashmolean Museum in Oxford came to Diamond to learn more about a 2,000-year-old prehistoric artifact. Using the microfocus beamline at I18, researchers unlocked new insights into Iron Age craft techniques and were able to redetermine the item's date.

science.title: Study finds families raising autistic children show resilience alongside higher stress
science.summary: Families raising a child with autism may experience greater levels of stress, but new University of Kentucky research published in the journal Autism suggests that is only part of the story. The study, led by Amanda Duncan, Ph.D., in the College of Education, found that families raising autistic children reported not only greater stress but also greater resilience. When researchers compared families experiencing similar levels of stress, those raising an autistic child demonstrated greater resilience.

science.title: Newly discovered orange killifish in the Brazilian Amazon may already be endangered
science.summary: Researchers have discovered a new species of brilliantly colored fish from a network of forest streams in the Brazilian Amazon and have already recommended it for listing as Endangered because of the pressures facing its only known home.

science.title: Follow the fish: How marine life is helping reveal hidden shipwrecks
science.summary: In September 2026, 20 Australian university students departed Brisbane for Fiji aboard the CSIRO research vessel (RV) Investigator on a CAPSTAN sea training voyage. While in coastal waters off Queensland, the students were involved in several shipwreck surveys that led to an intriguing observation: A shipwreck surrounded by mysterious holes on the seafloor. For some aboard, this wasn't the first time they'd seen such a thing.

science.title: Five ways teachers can respond to residential school denialism in the classroom
science.summary: Residential school denialism is entering or circulating within school communities across Canada in worrisome ways.

science.title: Liquid crystal takes page from steel in surprising phase transition
science.summary: A type of transformation best known for hardening steel and enabling shape-memory alloys may also occur in a much softer class of materials, according to new research from Rice University. Researchers in the departments of chemistry and chemical and biomolecular engineering and at the Smalley-Curl Institute at Rice have shown that an organic semiconductor can transform from a liquid crystal into a solid crystal through a rapid, highly coordinated process resembling a martensitic transformation—a phenomenon traditionally associated with changes between two solid crystalline structures.

science.title: Children's sport is great at keeping them busy—but are they learning?
science.summary: When families look into getting their children involved in sports and physical activities, there is often a lot to consider. For some, this means choosing between clubs and activities. For others, cost, transportation or availability can make organized sports harder to access. But there is another question we might rarely ask: What will my child actually experience and learn when they get there?

science.title: Quantum protocol securely verifies a device's position using stations 2 km apart
science.summary: Reliably verifying the location of a device connected to the internet or other networks is important for various real-world applications. For instance, it could be valuable for authorizing financial transactions, securing communications and controlling who can access specific databases or services.

science.title: Rope, twine and thread: Invisible technologies of the Stone Age
science.summary: When an abstract-looking ivory artifact emerged from the Hohle Fels cave in southern Germany in 2015, archaeologists didn't know quite what to make of it. Previously, the same cave had yielded what may be the world's oldest musical flutes, as well as one of humanity's earliest pieces of figurative art, the iconic Venus of Hohle Fels. At first glance, this strange new discovery—a 20-centimeter (8-inch) rod perforated with four small holes—seemed comparatively unspectacular.

science.title: For the first time, scientists watch sound jump between quantum states
science.summary: Stanford researchers have recorded the first real-time quantum jumps of sound, watching single phonons abruptly vanish from one energy state to another. The breakthrough could open new paths for quantum computing, error correction, highly sensitive biological sensors, and next-generation sound-based devices.

science.title: Carbon nanotube foams reveal a new kind of mechanical memory
science.summary: In their earliest years of development, computers used mechanical gears and levers to store information. Today, researchers are exploring whether a material itself can hold onto information, storing memory in how it bends and springs back to its original shape.

science.title: Bacteria-killing polymers—a new class of antibiotic?
science.summary: Swimming in the blood, sweat, cells and tears of every human are small proteins known as peptides. Many peptides can kill bacteria on contact, yet the bacteria never seem to evolve resistance to them. Mass-produced peptides could become a new type of antibiotic that evades resistance, but they are challenging to work with. They are short-lived and expensive to synthesize.

science.title: The state of sex among Gen Z: Is the sex recession real?
science.summary: The Kinsey Institute surveyed 2,373 U.S. adults ages 18–29 to understand attitudes and behaviors behind the so-called sex recession and how young adults are navigating sex, dating and relationships today.

science.title: Five foods that could cost even more this winter—and why
science.summary: A number of pressures have converged on food production over the past year, and their effects are likely to show up in our shopping carts this winter. Farmers have faced increasingly erratic weather, influenced by climate change and the El Niño phenomenon, while international conflicts have pushed up the cost of fuel, fertilizer and other essential inputs.

science.title: Invasive deer, goats are eating away Hawaiʻi's ranchlands
science.summary: The first study to measure wild ungulate (axis deer, mouflon sheep, goats, pigs, etc.) grazing on Hawaiʻi rangelands finds forage losses at two-thirds of sites surveyed, with axis deer the clearest driver of decline across ranches on Hawaiʻi Island and Maui.

science.title: Brazil has made gains against Amazon deforestation, but lasting protection is a challenge
science.summary: Recent drops in Brazil's deforestation have been celebrated as a historic achievement. Forest loss in the Amazon fell by 23.5% in 2025 compared with the previous year. This drop contributed to a 21% national reduction in overall clear-cutting—the lowest level recorded since 2016.

science.title: This new concrete is stronger and pulls CO2 from the air
science.summary: Researchers have created a concrete mixture that is both stronger and capable of absorbing carbon dioxide. The best formula, combining zeolite with bamboo biochar, boosted compressive strength by 7.48% and tensile strength by 15% compared with conventional concrete. It also captured about 1.2 grams of CO₂ per day in laboratory testing.

science.title: Water-based process separates zirconium and hafnium with fivefold higher efficiency
science.summary: Oregon State University scientists have patented a better, more environmentally friendly process for separating two metals that are critical in their pure forms for the semiconductor and atomic energy industries.

science.title: More social media use linked to poorer sleep and self-rated health among college students
science.summary: College students who spend more time on social media tend to sleep worse, and that may have consequences for how they perceive their own health, according to a new George Mason University study.

science.title: New study finds personality is key in hiring effective leaders
science.summary: A new study from Michigan State University found that the personality characteristics that get you promoted to a leadership role aren't necessarily the qualities that make you a good leader.

science.title: A strange circle on satellite maps turned out to be a 390-million-year-old impact crater
science.summary: An amateur astronomer searching satellite maps for a Quebec camping spot accidentally discovered a massive ancient impact crater. Scientists later found shatter cones that confirmed the 25-kilometer-wide structure was blasted into Earth roughly 390 million years ago.

science.title: Astronomers just found the youngest known planet ever
science.summary: Astronomers have confirmed a Jupiter-size planet less than a million years old, making Elias 2-24 b the youngest known planet and giving scientists a rare look at a world still being born. Its surprisingly rapid formation challenges leading theories about how giant planets come together, especially so far from their stars.

environment.title: Indigenous land back in Chile brings mixed bag of environmental outcomes: Study
environment.summary: Indigenous land restitution in Chile came with a mixed bag of environmental outcomes and did not boost natural forest cover, according to a new study published in Nature Sustainability. While the return of ancestral lands gave the Indigenous Mapuche communities in southern Chile greater control over how their land was used — leading to an […]

environment.title: 1.4-million-year-old footprints reveal a surprisingly large human relative
environment.summary: Ancient footprints in Kenya reveal that eight Paranthropus boisei may have traveled together 1.4 million years ago, with some individuals reaching surprisingly large, human-like body sizes. The tracks offer a rare glimpse of their social behavior and suggest these extinct human relatives may have lived in more complex groups than previously thought.

environment.title: Seven new frog species were hiding beneath Madagascar’s forest floor
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered seven new species of Madagascar’s elusive diamond frogs, using DNA from modern and century-old museum specimens to solve a long-running biological puzzle. The findings reveal surprising hidden diversity and could help protect these little-known amphibians as their forest habitats disappear.

environment.title: Ancient Egyptian princesses were buried with weapons. Their bones reveal why
environment.summary: Weapons buried with ancient Egyptian princesses may have been more than ceremonial decorations. Researchers studying royal mummies from Dahshur found bone changes consistent with years of archery and other strenuous weapon use. Several women also showed evidence of healed injuries, suggesting surprisingly active lifestyles that may have included hunting or military training.

environment.title: A Manhattan-sized ice island just broke free from Greenland
environment.summary: A huge section of Greenland’s Petermann Glacier has snapped off, forming an ice island about the size of Manhattan. Satellites watched cracks spread rapidly before the 76-square-kilometer slab finally broke free on August 4. It is the glacier’s biggest calving event since 2012, and scientists say two even larger pieces could eventually follow. The rare Arctic iceberg will now be tracked as it drifts, breaks apart, and potentially affects shipping routes.

environment.title: Atomic catalyst unlocks the hidden value of plant waste
environment.summary: Scientists have created a highly efficient catalyst that breaks down stubborn lignin from plant waste into useful chemicals under relatively mild conditions. By revealing exactly how the catalyst works at the atomic level, the discovery could help turn forestry and agricultural waste into renewable building blocks for fuels, plastics, and other materials.

environment.title: Scientists find hidden “highways” guiding animal evolution
environment.summary: A sweeping analysis of thousands of animal genomes suggests that chromosomes do not evolve randomly but instead follow a limited number of irreversible “evolutionary highways.” These one-way genetic changes preserve clues to more than 600 million years of animal history and could even help researchers explore where evolution may head next.

environment.title: NASA finds Earth microbes could survive on the Moon
environment.summary: NASA scientists found that microbes brought by astronauts could survive in cold, shadowed niches around the Moon’s South Pole, potentially complicating future searches for pristine lunar chemistry. Some refuges may be no larger than a footprint, while one hardy fungus could even withstand limited exposure to sunlight.

mix_items.summary: More than 170,000 respiratory cases were recorded in regions affected by haze in Indonesia, a Health Ministry official said Tuesday, as the country has battled for weeks to control fires that caused the toxic smog.

mix_items.summary: Research from stem cell charity Anthony Nolan, published in Transplantation and Cellular Therapy, has revealed that 1 in 50 people studied has an "especially useful" gene variant that could make them a particularly desirable stem cell donor.

mix_items.title: Why repeated exposures may make allergies worse
mix_items.summary: A new preclinical study led by investigators from Mass General Brigham offers a potential explanation for two longstanding questions in allergy: Why do allergies often emerge only after repeated exposure, and why do people with one allergy frequently develop others? The findings are published in Immunity.

mix_items.title: New tool aims to deliver graziers a faster, more accurate read on exactly how much feed is in front of their cattle
mix_items.summary: A drone lifts off over a paddock at Boorowa Agricultural Research Station, the breeze from its rotors setting the tall, uncut grass below rippling. At the controls, Stuart Brown, a senior research technician at CSIRO, keeps a careful eye on the attached LiDAR (Light Detection and Ranging) sensor as it fires an invisible lattice of laser pulses at the grass, building a three-dimensional map of the paddock, one small cube of space at a time.

mix_items.title: A tiny chariot fitting reveals Egyptian glass reached Iron Age Britain
mix_items.summary: At the end of last year, curators from the Ashmolean Museum in Oxford came to Diamond to learn more about a 2,000-year-old prehistoric artifact. Using the microfocus beamline at I18, researchers unlocked new insights into Iron Age craft techniques and were able to redetermine the item's date.

mix_items.title: AI assistant learns from radiology reports to spot problems in abdominal scans
mix_items.summary: An abdominal CT scan packs an extraordinary amount of information into a single image, layering dozens of organs and hundreds of possible conditions. It's widely considered one of the most complex scans in medicine to read, and even expert radiologists need time to carefully untangle what they're looking at. To help ease some of their workload, researchers presented a new AI assistant called RADAR (Rapid Abdominal Diagnosis with AI and Radiology).

mix_items.title: Study finds families raising autistic children show resilience alongside higher stress
mix_items.summary: Families raising a child with autism may experience greater levels of stress, but new University of Kentucky research published in the journal Autism suggests that is only part of the story. The study, led by Amanda Duncan, Ph.D., in the College of Education, found that families raising autistic children reported not only greater stress but also greater resilience. When researchers compared families experiencing similar levels of stress, those raising an autistic child demonstrated greater resilience.

mix_items.title: Newly discovered orange killifish in the Brazilian Amazon may already be endangered
mix_items.summary: Researchers have discovered a new species of brilliantly colored fish from a network of forest streams in the Brazilian Amazon and have already recommended it for listing as Endangered because of the pressures facing its only known home.

mix_items.title: Follow the fish: How marine life is helping reveal hidden shipwrecks
mix_items.summary: In September 2026, 20 Australian university students departed Brisbane for Fiji aboard the CSIRO research vessel (RV) Investigator on a CAPSTAN sea training voyage. While in coastal waters off Queensland, the students were involved in several shipwreck surveys that led to an intriguing observation: A shipwreck surrounded by mysterious holes on the seafloor. For some aboard, this wasn't the first time they'd seen such a thing.

mix_items.title: Five ways teachers can respond to residential school denialism in the classroom
mix_items.summary: Residential school denialism is entering or circulating within school communities across Canada in worrisome ways.

mix_items.title: Medicine leaflets are failing patients—and sometimes frightening them
mix_items.summary: Patient information leaflets are meant to help people use their medicines safely. But many people find them confusing, overwhelming or even frightening. If a document designed to keep people safe ends up putting them off their treatment, it's a sign that something isn't working.

mix_items.title: Liquid crystal takes page from steel in surprising phase transition
mix_items.summary: A type of transformation best known for hardening steel and enabling shape-memory alloys may also occur in a much softer class of materials, according to new research from Rice University. Researchers in the departments of chemistry and chemical and biomolecular engineering and at the Smalley-Curl Institute at Rice have shown that an organic semiconductor can transform from a liquid crystal into a solid crystal through a rapid, highly coordinated process resembling a martensitic transformation—a phenomenon traditionally associated with changes between two solid crystalline structures.

mix_items.title: Changing the way we age: Discovery could help preserve muscle strength
mix_items.summary: A groundbreaking discovery at the University of Missouri could help older adults maintain the muscle strength they need to stay active and independent, whether that means safely crossing the street or playing with their grandchildren.

mix_items.title: Lower spinal bone density may flag people at risk for cognitive decline
mix_items.summary: Researchers at Johns Hopkins University found that lower bone mineral density in the spine was associated with faster cognitive decline and accelerated age-related white matter injury, according to a study published in Radiology.

mix_items.title: Coffee doesn’t have to keep you awake to disrupt your sleep
mix_items.summary: Caffeine may make sleep less restorative even when you fall asleep normally and stay in bed for eight hours, with EEG recordings revealing fewer of the slow brain waves associated with deep sleep. Individual sensitivity varies dramatically, meaning even caffeine consumed earlier in the day could affect nighttime recovery for some people.

mix_items.title: 'Reporter game' helps regulate sensory-brain activity in autistic youth, MRI study finds
mix_items.summary: For many autistic children, everyday sensations such as the feel of scratchy fabric or a loud car alarm can be intensely distressing. Known as sensory over-responsivity, this common symptom can affect all aspects of everyday life, from school and family life to friendships, yet few research-based treatments exist.

mix_items.title: Children's sport is great at keeping them busy—but are they learning?
mix_items.summary: When families look into getting their children involved in sports and physical activities, there is often a lot to consider. For some, this means choosing between clubs and activities. For others, cost, transportation or availability can make organized sports harder to access. But there is another question we might rarely ask: What will my child actually experience and learn when they get there?

mix_items.title: Quantum protocol securely verifies a device's position using stations 2 km apart
mix_items.summary: Reliably verifying the location of a device connected to the internet or other networks is important for various real-world applications. For instance, it could be valuable for authorizing financial transactions, securing communications and controlling who can access specific databases or services.

mix_items.title: Varenicline and combination nicotine replacement therapy deemed preferred treatments for tobacco use
mix_items.summary: A new clinical practice guideline from the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) and Department of Defense (DoD) provides recommendations for tobacco use treatment. Tobacco and nicotine use among veterans and military service members causes physical and mental health effects and reduces force readiness.

mix_items.title: Rope, twine and thread: Invisible technologies of the Stone Age
mix_items.summary: When an abstract-looking ivory artifact emerged from the Hohle Fels cave in southern Germany in 2015, archaeologists didn't know quite what to make of it. Previously, the same cave had yielded what may be the world's oldest musical flutes, as well as one of humanity's earliest pieces of figurative art, the iconic Venus of Hohle Fels. At first glance, this strange new discovery—a 20-centimeter (8-inch) rod perforated with four small holes—seemed comparatively unspectacular.

mix_items.title: For the first time, scientists watch sound jump between quantum states
mix_items.summary: Stanford researchers have recorded the first real-time quantum jumps of sound, watching single phonons abruptly vanish from one energy state to another. The breakthrough could open new paths for quantum computing, error correction, highly sensitive biological sensors, and next-generation sound-based devices.

mix_items.title: Carbon nanotube foams reveal a new kind of mechanical memory
mix_items.summary: In their earliest years of development, computers used mechanical gears and levers to store information. Today, researchers are exploring whether a material itself can hold onto information, storing memory in how it bends and springs back to its original shape.

mix_items.title: Bacteria-killing polymers—a new class of antibiotic?
mix_items.summary: Swimming in the blood, sweat, cells and tears of every human are small proteins known as peptides. Many peptides can kill bacteria on contact, yet the bacteria never seem to evolve resistance to them. Mass-produced peptides could become a new type of antibiotic that evades resistance, but they are challenging to work with. They are short-lived and expensive to synthesize.

mix_items.title: Women with enlarged breast tissue more likely to experience chronic migraine, neck pain and sleep apnea
mix_items.summary: Women with enlarged breast tissue, known medically as macromastia, may be more likely to experience chronic migraine, neck pain, certain spinal nerve disorders and obstructive sleep apnea, according to a new study by Wake Forest University School of Medicine researchers, published Tuesday in the journal Headache.

mix_items.title: The state of sex among Gen Z: Is the sex recession real?
mix_items.summary: The Kinsey Institute surveyed 2,373 U.S. adults ages 18–29 to understand attitudes and behaviors behind the so-called sex recession and how young adults are navigating sex, dating and relationships today.

mix_items.title: Five foods that could cost even more this winter—and why
mix_items.summary: A number of pressures have converged on food production over the past year, and their effects are likely to show up in our shopping carts this winter. Farmers have faced increasingly erratic weather, influenced by climate change and the El Niño phenomenon, while international conflicts have pushed up the cost of fuel, fertilizer and other essential inputs.

mix_items.title: Engineered probiotic bacteria produce cancer drugs inside tumors
mix_items.summary: E. coli in uncooked meat can cause diarrhea and food poisoning. Scientists, however, have found a way to turn the bacterium into a delivery agent that takes drugs straight to a tumor and transforms it into a tiny cancer drug dispensary.

mix_items.title: More than a third of positive tests for mpox may have been false diagnoses
mix_items.summary: In August 2024, the World Health Organization declared the mpox upsurge in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and its spread to neighboring countries a Public Health Emergency of International Concern. The emergence of a new strain and its rapid spread across eastern DRC, and later to other African countries and beyond, made reliable diagnosis essential for understanding the scale of the epidemic and guiding vaccination and other public health measures.

mix_items.title: Invasive deer, goats are eating away Hawaiʻi's ranchlands
mix_items.summary: The first study to measure wild ungulate (axis deer, mouflon sheep, goats, pigs, etc.) grazing on Hawaiʻi rangelands finds forage losses at two-thirds of sites surveyed, with axis deer the clearest driver of decline across ranches on Hawaiʻi Island and Maui.

mix_items.title: What kind of a person am I? How fear and rejection can underpin OCD
mix_items.summary: When you think about obsessive-compulsive disorder, or OCD, does being a "neat freak" or "germophobe" come to mind?

mix_items.title: Brazil has made gains against Amazon deforestation, but lasting protection is a challenge
mix_items.summary: Recent drops in Brazil's deforestation have been celebrated as a historic achievement. Forest loss in the Amazon fell by 23.5% in 2025 compared with the previous year. This drop contributed to a 21% national reduction in overall clear-cutting—the lowest level recorded since 2016.

mix_items.title: Study identifies estrogen receptor as key protector of the right heart in pulmonary hypertension
mix_items.summary: Researchers at National Jewish Health have identified a key way estrogen receptor alpha (ERα) helps protect the right side of the heart in pulmonary hypertension. The preclinical findings reveal that ERα preserves the survival and movement of endothelial cells, which line blood vessels, allowing the stressed heart to maintain the small vessels it needs to function.

mix_items.title: This new concrete is stronger and pulls CO2 from the air
mix_items.summary: Researchers have created a concrete mixture that is both stronger and capable of absorbing carbon dioxide. The best formula, combining zeolite with bamboo biochar, boosted compressive strength by 7.48% and tensile strength by 15% compared with conventional concrete. It also captured about 1.2 grams of CO₂ per day in laboratory testing.

mix_items.title: Water-based process separates zirconium and hafnium with fivefold higher efficiency
mix_items.summary: Oregon State University scientists have patented a better, more environmentally friendly process for separating two metals that are critical in their pure forms for the semiconductor and atomic energy industries.

mix_items.title: More social media use linked to poorer sleep and self-rated health among college students
mix_items.summary: College students who spend more time on social media tend to sleep worse, and that may have consequences for how they perceive their own health, according to a new George Mason University study.

mix_items.title: Researchers highlight how brain economy principles could transform clinical care
mix_items.summary: Researchers from The University of Texas Medical Branch (UTMB) are helping advance a growing global movement that reimagines health care through the lens of brain health.

mix_items.title: New study finds personality is key in hiring effective leaders
mix_items.summary: A new study from Michigan State University found that the personality characteristics that get you promoted to a leadership role aren't necessarily the qualities that make you a good leader.

mix_items.title: Patients with chronic pain may benefit from group medical visits
mix_items.summary: More than one in five U.S. adults lives with chronic pain, which isolation and stigma can worsen. Group medical visits allow multiple patients with a common condition to receive care alongside health education and peer support.

mix_items.title: A strange circle on satellite maps turned out to be a 390-million-year-old impact crater
mix_items.summary: An amateur astronomer searching satellite maps for a Quebec camping spot accidentally discovered a massive ancient impact crater. Scientists later found shatter cones that confirmed the 25-kilometer-wide structure was blasted into Earth roughly 390 million years ago.

mix_items.title: Indigenous land back in Chile brings mixed bag of environmental outcomes: Study
mix_items.summary: Indigenous land restitution in Chile came with a mixed bag of environmental outcomes and did not boost natural forest cover, according to a new study published in Nature Sustainability. While the return of ancestral lands gave the Indigenous Mapuche communities in southern Chile greater control over how their land was used — leading to an […]

mix_items.title: Astronomers just found the youngest known planet ever
mix_items.summary: Astronomers have confirmed a Jupiter-size planet less than a million years old, making Elias 2-24 b the youngest known planet and giving scientists a rare look at a world still being born. Its surprisingly rapid formation challenges leading theories about how giant planets come together, especially so far from their stars.

mix_items.title: Scientists find a natural gut compound that helps heal the intestine
mix_items.summary: A natural compound produced by gut bacteria after digesting foods such as pomegranates, walnuts, and berries may help repair and protect the intestinal lining. The discovery reveals a surprising beneficial side of an inflammatory pathway and could inspire more targeted treatments for Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis.

mix_items.title: Textbooks may have misdrawn this basic brain structure for 100 years
mix_items.summary: Scientists discovered that brain-cell axons may not be smooth tubes as textbooks have shown for more than a century, but instead naturally resemble strings of tiny pearls. Those pearl-like structures can change with neural activity and may help control how quickly electrical signals travel through the brain.

mix_items.title: 51 ways to get the planet tipping the right way

mix_items.title: 1.4-million-year-old footprints reveal a surprisingly large human relative
mix_items.summary: Ancient footprints in Kenya reveal that eight Paranthropus boisei may have traveled together 1.4 million years ago, with some individuals reaching surprisingly large, human-like body sizes. The tracks offer a rare glimpse of their social behavior and suggest these extinct human relatives may have lived in more complex groups than previously thought.

mix_items.title: Seven new frog species were hiding beneath Madagascar’s forest floor
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered seven new species of Madagascar’s elusive diamond frogs, using DNA from modern and century-old museum specimens to solve a long-running biological puzzle. The findings reveal surprising hidden diversity and could help protect these little-known amphibians as their forest habitats disappear.

mix_items.title: Ancient Egyptian princesses were buried with weapons. Their bones reveal why
mix_items.summary: Weapons buried with ancient Egyptian princesses may have been more than ceremonial decorations. Researchers studying royal mummies from Dahshur found bone changes consistent with years of archery and other strenuous weapon use. Several women also showed evidence of healed injuries, suggesting surprisingly active lifestyles that may have included hunting or military training.

mix_items.title: A Manhattan-sized ice island just broke free from Greenland
mix_items.summary: A huge section of Greenland’s Petermann Glacier has snapped off, forming an ice island about the size of Manhattan. Satellites watched cracks spread rapidly before the 76-square-kilometer slab finally broke free on August 4. It is the glacier’s biggest calving event since 2012, and scientists say two even larger pieces could eventually follow. The rare Arctic iceberg will now be tracked as it drifts, breaks apart, and potentially affects shipping routes.

mix_items.title: Atomic catalyst unlocks the hidden value of plant waste
mix_items.summary: Scientists have created a highly efficient catalyst that breaks down stubborn lignin from plant waste into useful chemicals under relatively mild conditions. By revealing exactly how the catalyst works at the atomic level, the discovery could help turn forestry and agricultural waste into renewable building blocks for fuels, plastics, and other materials.

mix_items.title: Scientists find hidden “highways” guiding animal evolution
mix_items.summary: A sweeping analysis of thousands of animal genomes suggests that chromosomes do not evolve randomly but instead follow a limited number of irreversible “evolutionary highways.” These one-way genetic changes preserve clues to more than 600 million years of animal history and could even help researchers explore where evolution may head next.

mix_items.title: NASA finds Earth microbes could survive on the Moon
mix_items.summary: NASA scientists found that microbes brought by astronauts could survive in cold, shadowed niches around the Moon’s South Pole, potentially complicating future searches for pristine lunar chemistry. Some refuges may be no larger than a footprint, while one hardy fungus could even withstand limited exposure to sunlight.
